q: A script runs `rm -r build/`. Which build/ does it delete?
choices: The one in the folder the script is run from
The one next to the script file
The one in your home folder
explain: A path without a leading / is relative: it starts from the folder you are in when you run the script (shown by pwd), not from where the script file lives. Run it from your home and it deletes ~/build. Safe scripts first cd to a known folder, or use full paths like /srv/app/build.

q: A tutorial says `curl https://get.example.sh | sudo bash`. What is the risk?
choices: You run code you never read, as root
curl downloads too slowly for bash
bash cannot read a script from a pipe
explain: The pipe sends whatever the site returns straight into a root shell: you never see it, and it can do anything to the machine. HTTPS only proves which site sent it, not what the script does. Safer: curl -o install.sh URL, read it (less install.sh), then run it.

q: Why don't .bashrc or .ssh show up in a plain `ls`?
choices: Names starting with a dot are hidden
They are links, ls skips links
explain: On Linux, a file whose name starts with a dot is hidden: ls skips it to keep the listing tidy. It is not protected, just not shown. ls -a (all) shows them. Your settings live there (.bashrc, .ssh), and so do things an intruder may leave behind: look with ls -a.

q: Why do scripts write `mkdir -p logs` rather than `mkdir logs`?
choices: It doesn't fail when logs already exists
It creates it in your home
explain: mkdir logs stops with an error if logs already exists, so the second run of the script fails. mkdir -p is happy either way, and also creates missing parent folders (mkdir -p a/b/c). A good script can run twice without breaking: that is called idempotent.

q: You want to add a line to /etc/hosts without losing the rest. Which do you use?
explain: >> adds at the end of the file and keeps what is already there. A single > empties the file first, then writes: one wrong > and /etc/hosts is gone. | sends output to another command, < reads a file as input. Tip: set -o noclobber makes > refuse to overwrite an existing file.

q: `grep error app.log | wc -l` prints 12. What is 12?
choices: The number of lines that contain error
The number of times error appears
The number of lines in app.log
explain: grep prints each line that contains error; the pipe | hands those lines to wc -l, which counts lines. So 12 lines have the word at least once. A line with error twice still counts once. grep -c error app.log gives the same count on its own.

q: How do you find a long command you typed yesterday?
choices: Ctrl+R, then type a piece of it
explain: Ctrl+R searches your history backwards as you type: press Ctrl+R again for older matches, Enter to run, → to edit first. The history is saved in ~/.bash_history. Careful: a password typed on a command line is saved there too.

q: You forgot a command's options. Where is the reliable answer, even offline?
explain: The help installed with the tool describes exactly the version you have; a forum answer may be for another version or another system. cmd --help gives a short summary, man cmd the full manual: / searches in it, n goes to the next match, q quits.

q: A script must know whether `cp` worked. What does it look at?
explain: Every command ends with a number called its exit code: 0 means success, anything else is an error. Many commands print nothing when all is well, so silence proves nothing. echo $? shows the last code, and if cp a b; then … else … fi tests it directly.

q: Why is `mysql -pSecret123` a bad way to give a password?
choices: It lands in your history and shows in ps
explain: The whole command line, password included, is saved in your shell history, and while it runs any user on the machine can read it with ps. Better: type -p alone and let mysql ask for the password, or put it in a config file only you can read (chmod 600).

q: rm has no trash. What's a good habit before `rm *.log`?
choices: Run `ls *.log` first to see what matches
explain: Before rm even starts, bash replaces *.log with the list of matching names. ls *.log does the same replacement, so it shows exactly what rm would delete. -f only removes the safety questions, and -r would also go into folders: both make a mistake worse.

q: What is stderr for?
choices: Error messages, kept apart from the real output
explain: A command has two outputs: stdout (number 1) for its results and stderr (number 2) for errors and warnings. Keeping them apart means cmd > out.txt saves only the results in the file while errors still show on screen, and 2> errors.txt saves the errors on their own.

q: `cut -d' ' -f3 people.txt | uniq -c` shows nantes on three separate lines. Why?
choices: uniq only merges identical lines that are next to each other
cut left a space after some cities
explain: uniq compares each line with the one just before it, nothing more. When the nantes lines are spread through the file, each one starts a new group. Put sort before it: cut -d' ' -f3 people.txt | sort | uniq -c. sort puts identical lines side by side, then uniq counts each group once.

q: `sort scores.txt` puts 100 before 9, and 95 after 120. What is going on?
choices: sort compares text; sort -n compares numbers
sort only looks at the last digit
explain: By default sort compares lines as text, character by character, like words in a dictionary: '1' comes before '9', so 100 comes before 9. -n tells sort to read each line as a number. Add -r to get the biggest first: sort -rn scores.txt | head -3 gives the top three.

q: A cron job's errors vanish. Which line logs them along with the output?
explain: Redirections are read left to right. >> job.log sends stdout to the file, then 2>&1 says: send stderr where stdout goes now, the file. In the other order, 2>&1 copies stdout while it still points to the screen, so errors never reach the log. Cron has no screen: those errors are lost.

q: A backup script writes `backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz`. Which name comes out?
choices: An error: date is not a variable
explain: $( ) runs the command inside and puts its output in its place, before the rest runs: this is command substitution. date +%F prints the date as YYYY-MM-DD. That format sorts in date order with a plain ls, handy for backups. In single quotes it would stay as written.

q: Which loop still works when file names contain spaces?
choices: for f in *.log; do gzip "$f"; done
for f in $(ls *.log); do gzip $f; done
ls *.log | for f; do gzip $f; done
for f in "$(ls)"; do gzip "$f"; done
explain: *.log gives one item per file, even when the name has spaces. $(ls) produces text that bash then cuts at every space, so 'my app.log' becomes two wrong names. Then "$f" in quotes passes the name as one piece. Habit: loop over a glob, and always quote your variables.

q: Why start a script with `set -euo pipefail`?
choices: It stops at a failed command, unset variable or broken pipe
It runs the script as root
explain: By default bash carries on after an error. -e stops at the first failed command, -u stops on a variable that was never set (a typo becomes an error, not an empty string), -o pipefail makes a pipe fail if any part fails. Without them, a failed cd is followed by an rm in the wrong folder.

q: How do you read a file line by line safely?
choices: while IFS= read -r line; do …; done < file
explain: read reads one whole line at a time, and < file feeds it the file. IFS= keeps spaces at the start and end of the line, -r keeps backslashes as they are. for line in $(cat file) cuts the text at every space, so you get words, not lines.

q: Why write `cd /srv/app && rm -rf ./cache` rather than using `;`?
choices: If cd fails, rm doesn't run in the wrong folder
explain: && runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded. If /srv/app doesn't exist, cd fails and rm -rf never runs. With ; the rm runs anyway, in whatever folder you were in. || is the opposite: it runs only after a failure (cmd || echo failed).

q: f='old notes.txt'. What does `rm $f` do?
choices: Tries to delete two files: old and notes.txt
Fails: the variable needs quotes inside
explain: Without quotes, bash cuts the variable's value at spaces before running the command: rm receives two names, old and notes.txt. If a file called old exists, it goes. Written rm "$f", the value stays one piece. Quote every variable unless you really want it cut.

q: `./deploy.sh` says Permission denied, yet you own it. Why?
explain: Owning a file doesn't make it runnable: it needs the x (execute) permission, visible in ls -l as -rwxr-xr-x. chmod +x deploy.sh adds it. bash deploy.sh also works, since bash then only reads the file. On a disk mounted noexec, ./ never works.

q: How does a script remove its temp file even when it fails half way?
choices: An rm on its last line
explain: trap 'command' EXIT registers a command that bash runs whenever the script ends: normal end, an error with set -e, or Ctrl+C. An rm on the last line never runs if the script stops earlier. Usual pair: tmp=$(mktemp) then trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT.

q: Why use `tmp=$(mktemp)` instead of a fixed /tmp/myscript.tmp?
choices: Another user could create or link that fixed name first
explain: Every user can write in /tmp. If someone creates /tmp/myscript.tmp first, for example as a link to one of your files, your script writes into that file instead. mktemp creates a new file with a random name that only you can read, so nobody can prepare the trap in advance.

q: You want the 3 most frequent lines of access.log, with their counts. Which pipeline gives them?
explain: Read it step by step: sort groups identical lines, uniq -c turns each group into one line with its count, sort -rn orders those counts from biggest to smallest, head -3 keeps the top three. Without the first sort, uniq counts the same line several times. It's one of the most useful pipelines for reading logs.

q: You opened notes.txt with vi and started typing, but the letters do strange things instead of appearing. Why?
choices: It's in normal mode, where keys are commands: i to type
The terminal is broken: close it
explain: vi has two modes. It opens in normal mode, where each key is a command (dd deletes a line, x a character). Press i to enter insert mode and type; Esc goes back. If you got lost, Esc then :q! quits without saving anything, and you can start again.

q: You changed a config file in nano and press Ctrl+X. nano asks "Save modified buffer?". What is it telling you?
choices: Your changes aren't saved: Y saves them, N drops them
You must be root to quit
nano wants a backup copy first
explain: "Buffer" is nano's word for the text you're editing. It warns you before quitting with unsaved changes: Y writes them (Enter confirms the file name), N drops them. Ctrl+O saves without quitting, handy to save often.

q: You want the lines of app.log that START with ERROR, not the ones that only mention it later. Which pattern?
explain: In a pattern, ^ means "the start of the line" and $ means "the end". '^ERROR' keeps only the lines that begin with it, so a message quoting the word later doesn't match. -v would do the opposite: keep the lines without ERROR.

q: Why write grep -E '[0-9]+' log.txt with the pattern in single quotes?
choices: So the shell leaves [ ] and + alone for grep
grep only reads patterns in quotes
To search for the quote characters too
explain: The shell reads your line before grep runs, and [ ], * and ? mean something to it too (file name patterns). Inside single quotes the shell changes nothing, so grep gets exactly the pattern you wrote. It's a habit worth keeping for every regex, in grep, sed and awk.

q: You need every .log file under /var/log, in all its subfolders too. Which command finds them?
explain: find walks through a folder and every folder inside it, and keeps what matches: -name '*.log' matches the names. ls /var/log/*.log only looks one level down, in /var/log itself. grep searches inside files, not for file names.

q: Why put the pattern in quotes in find . -name '*.txt'?
choices: Unquoted, the shell may expand *.txt here before find runs
It's only a matter of style
explain: The shell expands * before running a command. If the current folder has notes.txt, an unquoted *.txt becomes notes.txt, and find then looks only for that name. With quotes, find gets the pattern itself and applies it in every folder.

q: Each line of access.txt looks like `alice 200 /home`. How do you print only the second column, the status code?
explain: awk splits each line into fields at the spaces: $1 is alice, $2 is 200, $3 is /home. '{print $2}' prints the second one for every line. grep 200 would print whole lines, and only those that contain 200 anywhere.

q: A colleague sends backup.tar.gz. What do you do before unpacking it where you stand?
choices: List what's inside with tar -tzf backup.tar.gz
Unpack it as root to be safe
explain: tar -t lists the content without writing anything. You see whether everything sits in one folder or would scatter dozens of files where you are, and whether a file would overwrite one of yours. Then unpack with tar -xzf, or add -C to choose the folder.

q: In git, what does a commit keep?
choices: A snapshot of what you added with git add, plus a message
Only the last line you changed
A copy sent to the server right away
explain: git add chooses which changes go in, git commit records them as one snapshot you can come back to, with who and why. Nothing leaves your machine until you git push. Small commits with clear messages make it easy to find when something broke.

q: You broke a file in a git repository and haven't committed yet. How do you get the last committed version back?
explain: git restore puts the file back as it was in the last commit, dropping the changes you made since. It's safe to experiment in a repository for this reason: git status shows what changed, git diff shows how, and git restore undoes it. The .git folder is the history itself: never delete it.

q: In sort --help, the line `-f, --ignore-case` says what?
choices: One option, two spellings: it ignores capitals
-f needs a file name right after it
sort ignores the file's case when it saves it
explain: Help pages list each option once, with its short form (one dash, one letter) and its long form (two dashes, a word), separated by a comma: they mean exactly the same. sort -f names.txt and sort --ignore-case names.txt give the same result. The long form is easier to read in a script, the short one faster to type.

q: You've changed a file in nano. Which keys save it and leave?
explain: nano lists its keys at the bottom of the screen; ^ means Ctrl. Ctrl+O writes the file Out (Enter confirms the name), Ctrl+X eXits. If you press Ctrl+X first, nano asks whether to save. :q belongs to vi, and it refuses to quit when there are unsaved changes: :wq saves and quits there.

q: photos/ exists. What does `mv beach.jpg cat.jpg photos/` do?
choices: Moves both files into photos/, with the same names
Copies both files and keeps the originals
Fails: mv takes only two names
explain: mv takes as many files as you like, and the last name is where they go. When that last name is a folder, the files move inside and keep their names. With only two names and no such folder, mv renames the first one. mv never keeps the original: that's cp.

q: The folder holds report-2025-01.csv, report-2024-01.csv and old-report-2025-02.csv. What does `rm report-2025-*.csv` remove?
explain: Bash turns the pattern into names before rm starts: * stands for any characters, but the rest of the pattern must match exactly, from the first letter. old-report-... doesn't start with report, and report-2024-... has 2024. Since rm has no undo, run ls report-2025-*.csv first: it shows exactly what rm would remove.
